heuristics.rule: Never disclose current salary before an offer is made — it can only anchor the negotiation downward
heuristics.condition: When any employer asks for your current or past compensation at any stage of the hiring process
heuristics.action: Redirect with: 'I prefer not to share my salary history, but I'm happy to discuss my compensation expectations for this role.'
heuristics.because: Disclosing a below-market salary gives the employer a ceiling to work from rather than their actual budget, structurally disadvantaging you in every subsequent negotiation step

heuristics.rule: If you're a remote worker, your protections follow your physical location, not the employer's headquarters
heuristics.condition: When interviewing remotely with a company headquartered in a non-ban state while you live in a ban state
heuristics.action: Invoke your state's salary history ban protections — they apply to you regardless of where the company is based
heuristics.because: Colorado, California, New York, and others explicitly extend their bans to cover employees located in those states even when the employer operates elsewhere

heuristics.rule: Use posted pay ranges as an opening anchor, not a ceiling
heuristics.condition: When a company is required to post salary ranges in job listings (California, Colorado, NY, etc.) and has done so
heuristics.action: Open with: 'I see the range is $X–$Y. Given my experience, I'm targeting the upper end of that range'
heuristics.because: A posted range tells you the actual budget; targeting the top of the range with justification is more powerful than guessing and more credible than demanding above range

heuristics.rule: If you already disclosed your salary, immediately reframe toward forward-looking expectations rather than defending the number
heuristics.condition: When you've already shared a below-market number — whether voluntarily or before knowing your rights
heuristics.action: In the next conversation, pivot: 'Now that we've discussed the role in more detail, I'm focused on [target range] for the offer' or cite market data to reframe
heuristics.because: Anchors can be disrupted by introducing new information or reframing the context; sitting passively on a low anchor compounds its damage across the entire offer

heuristics.rule: Document any salary history question asked in a ban state — date, interviewer, exact wording — before deciding how to respond
heuristics.condition: When an employer in a ban-state asks about your salary history despite the legal prohibition
heuristics.action: Document the violation immediately, then decide whether to escalate; the violation itself can become negotiation leverage
heuristics.because: Private rights to sue exist in California, Colorado, Illinois, Massachusetts, New York, and Washington, with remedies including back pay, wage differentials, and civil penalties up to $25,000

decision_factors.factor: Whether you are in a salary history ban state
decision_factors.why_it_matters: Determines whether you are legally protected from being asked about past compensation and whether you have legal recourse if asked
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Check the list of 22 states and 23+ municipalities; also check your remote work location, not just the employer's HQ location

decision_factors.factor: Whether the employer is required to post a pay range
decision_factors.why_it_matters: Posted ranges reveal actual budget and shift negotiating power to the candidate by eliminating information asymmetry
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Check if employer meets employee threshold in states like California (15+), Hawaii (50+), Illinois (15+), Maryland (all), Minnesota (30+), New York (4+), Washington (15+)

decision_factors.factor: Whether you have already voluntarily disclosed your salary
decision_factors.why_it_matters: Voluntary disclosure is explicitly exempt from ban protections; it cannot be legally contested after the fact, and creates a downward anchor
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Review whether you brought up the number unprompted or whether they asked first; the legal protection only applies when they solicited the information

decision_factors.factor: Which state law applies to your specific situation
decision_factors.why_it_matters: Some states (Michigan, Wisconsin) actively prohibit local governments from passing salary history bans, meaning there is zero protection even at the city level
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Identify your physical work location, then check both state-level bans and notable municipal exceptions; do not assume a ban applies without verifying

decision_factors.factor: Whether a private right to sue exists in your state
decision_factors.why_it_matters: Determines whether a violation is enforceable beyond filing a complaint — and whether a violation gives you real leverage in negotiation
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Private rights to sue confirmed in: California, Colorado, Illinois, Massachusetts, New York, Washington; other states may only allow labor department complaints

decision_factors.factor: Filing deadline for state labor complaints
decision_factors.why_it_matters: Missing the window eliminates your legal remedy entirely; deadlines range from 6 months to 3 years depending on state
decision_factors.how_to_assess: If you believe a violation occurred, check your state labor department's complaint deadline immediately — do not wait

decision_factors.factor: Whether the role is an internal promotion vs. new external hire
decision_factors.why_it_matters: Some states' salary history bans only cover new hires, meaning internal promotion negotiations may not carry the same legal protections
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Washington's ban explicitly covers internal promotions; check whether your state extends the ban beyond external hiring

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Disclosing your current salary when asked — even when legal — to appear cooperative or avoid awkwardness
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: The number becomes a hard anchor that bounds the offer regardless of the role's actual budget; even a generous employer will rarely offer far above a disclosed current salary
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Underpaid candidates, career changers moving to higher-paying industries, and anyone whose current comp is below market rate for the new role

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Not knowing your state's salary history ban status before interviewing
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: You may comply with an illegal question, forfeit your legal protections through voluntary disclosure, and lose negotiating leverage that the law was explicitly designed to give you
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: First-time job seekers and anyone relocating to a new state who hasn't updated their knowledge of local employment law

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Escalating a salary history ban violation to the state labor department or pursuing legal action
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: While legally valid, it almost certainly ends your candidacy with that employer and may create reputational risk in tight-knit industries or geographies
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Candidates who are actively job searching in a narrow industry where the employer has significant market presence

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Relying on a ban-state employer voluntarily following the law without knowing your rights
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: Violations are common; without knowing what's prohibited, you cannot recognize when a violation occurs, let alone document or respond to it
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Candidates who assume legal compliance without verification, particularly those earlier in their careers who treat recruiter questions as standard procedure

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Reframing a voluntarily disclosed low salary upward mid-process
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: While strategically sound, it can create friction with the recruiter and signal inconsistency — the reframe must be tied to new information (role scope, market data) to land credibly
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Candidates who disclosed early without leverage or context and are now trying to recover lost ground

failure_patterns.pattern: Answering the salary history question reflexively before knowing whether it's legal to ask
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Candidates treat recruiter questions as authoritative and feel social pressure to answer; disclosing feels cooperative while refusing feels adversarial
failure_patterns.consequence: Locks in a below-market anchor that the entire offer and negotiation is built around, often costing thousands to tens of thousands annually
warning_signs: You answered 'What are you currently making?' without pausing to consider whether you had to
You felt that refusing would 'hurt your chances' even in a state where the question was illegal

failure_patterns.pattern: Assuming the employer's headquarters location determines which state's employment law applies
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Most people think of their employer's location as the relevant legal jurisdiction; remote work has decoupled this assumption but not the mental model
failure_patterns.consequence: Candidates in ban states like New York or California interviewing with Texas or Florida companies waive protections they actually have
warning_signs: You work remotely but have never checked whether your state's laws apply to your out-of-state employer
You assumed no ban applied because the company is headquartered in a non-ban state

failure_patterns.pattern: Voluntarily disclosing salary history to 'get ahead of it' or appear transparent
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Candidates conflate general transparency as a value with strategic disclosure; they believe sharing builds rapport and reduces friction
failure_patterns.consequence: Voluntarily disclosed salary is explicitly exempt from ban-state protections, and the number anchors the offer regardless of intent
warning_signs: You volunteered your current salary before being asked
You included compensation history on an application form even when it was optional

failure_patterns.pattern: Failing to document a salary history ban violation in the moment
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Candidates are focused on the interview itself and don't think about legal compliance in real time; documentation feels like an escalation they're not ready to commit to
failure_patterns.consequence: Without documentation, you cannot file a complaint, cannot establish the violation occurred, and lose the legal leverage the violation would have given you
warning_signs: You remember being asked about salary history in a ban state but took no notes
You didn't record the interviewer's name, date, or exact phrasing of the question

failure_patterns.pattern: Sitting passively on a low salary anchor after early disclosure instead of reframing
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Candidates believe that revisiting a disclosed number looks inconsistent or desperate; they hope the employer will disregard it or be generous anyway
failure_patterns.consequence: The anchor compounds — every step of the offer process (base, bonus targets, equity refresh) is calibrated against the disclosed number rather than market rate
warning_signs: You shared a low number early and haven't introduced market data or role-scope context since
You're waiting for the offer to 'see what they come back with' rather than proactively resetting expectations

diagnostic_questions.question: What state do you physically live and work in — and is it different from the employer's headquarters?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Determines which state's salary history ban law applies and whether the candidate has legal protection they may not know about
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: Your state's law likely applies to you regardless of employer HQ — check whether your state has an active ban before your next interview
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: Check whether your state has a ban; if not, check for applicable municipal ordinances in your city

diagnostic_questions.question: Have you already disclosed your current or past salary at any point in this process?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Determines whether the anchor has already been set and what recovery strategy is available
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: Was it voluntary or in response to a direct question? If you're in a ban state and they asked, you may have documentation leverage. Either way, reframe forward immediately.
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: You have full negotiating flexibility — do not disclose before an offer is made

diagnostic_questions.question: Did the company post a salary range in the job listing, or are they required to by law in your state?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Reveals whether you already have the employer's budget information, which fundamentally changes your negotiation opening
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: Use the posted range as your anchor; open by targeting the upper end with explicit justification
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: You'll need to research market data from other sources (levels.fyi, Glassdoor, Blind, Bureau of Labor Statistics) to establish your target range independently

diagnostic_questions.question: Was the salary history question asked in writing (application form, email) or verbally in an interview?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Determines how easy it is to document the violation and the strength of evidence if you choose to escalate
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: Screenshot or save the written request immediately — written evidence substantially strengthens any complaint or legal action
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: Document immediately after the interview: date, interviewer name, exact wording recalled, any witnesses present

diagnostic_questions.question: Is this an internal promotion or an external new hire situation?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Some states' salary history bans only cover external hires, not internal compensation changes — this changes what protections apply
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: Check whether your state extends the ban to internal promotions (Washington does explicitly; most others may not)
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: Standard salary history ban protections for new hires apply if you're in a ban state

industry_realities.common_belief: If a recruiter asks you about your current salary, you are obligated to answer
industry_realities.actual_reality: In 22 states and 23+ municipalities, asking the question is illegal — the recruiter may not even know this, and candidates have the legal right to decline
industry_realities.implication: Candidates should know their state's status before any interview begins, and have a rehearsed redirect ready that doesn't create friction

industry_realities.common_belief: Laws about salary history only apply to employers headquartered in that state
industry_realities.actual_reality: Protections follow the employee's physical location — Colorado explicitly covers out-of-state companies with Colorado-based employees; California applies to remote workers located in California
industry_realities.implication: Remote workers in ban states are protected even when their employer is in Texas, Florida, or any other non-ban state

industry_realities.common_belief: Pay transparency laws (posting salary ranges) primarily benefit employers by setting expectations
industry_realities.actual_reality: They structurally shift negotiating power to candidates by revealing the employer's actual budget before any negotiation begins
industry_realities.implication: In states with posting requirements, candidates should always anchor to the top of the posted range with justification rather than guessing or anchoring low

industry_realities.common_belief: Voluntarily sharing your salary is protected the same way as being asked for it in a ban state
industry_realities.actual_reality: Voluntary disclosure is explicitly carved out as an exception in virtually all salary history ban laws — once you share it unprompted, the legal protection no longer applies to that information
industry_realities.implication: Never volunteer salary information before an offer, even in casual conversation or to 'set expectations' — the legal protection disappears the moment you bring it up first

industry_realities.common_belief: If an employer violates a salary history ban, there's nothing practical you can do
industry_realities.actual_reality: Six states (California, Colorado, Illinois, Massachusetts, New York, Washington) grant private rights to sue with remedies including back pay, wage differentials, attorney's fees, and civil penalties up to $25,000
industry_realities.implication: Documenting a violation in these states creates real legal leverage — not just a complaint mechanism — that can be carefully referenced in negotiation

industry_realities.common_belief: Michigan and Wisconsin just don't have salary history bans, like most states
industry_realities.actual_reality: Michigan and Wisconsin have laws that actively prohibit local governments from passing salary history bans — even municipalities cannot protect workers there
industry_realities.implication: Workers in these states have zero salary history protection at any level of government; full compensation history disclosure can be legally required

junior_vs_senior_signals.dimension: Response to the salary history question
junior_vs_senior_signals.junior_pattern: Answers reflexively, treating the recruiter's question as an obligation; may even volunteer current salary proactively to seem cooperative
junior_vs_senior_signals.senior_pattern: Redirects smoothly without hesitation: 'I prefer not to share my history, but I'm happy to discuss my expectations for this role' — prepared in advance
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Answering anchors every subsequent number in the process; redirecting preserves full negotiating range and signals market awareness

junior_vs_senior_signals.dimension: Knowledge of legal protections before interviewing
junior_vs_senior_signals.junior_pattern: Treats salary questions as standard practice; doesn't know which states have bans or that remote work location determines applicable law
junior_vs_senior_signals.senior_pattern: Checks ban status before the first recruiter screen; knows their state's law, whether the employer must post ranges, and what the right to refuse looks like
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Legal knowledge changes what you're willing to say and documents violations in real time — ignorance of the law means forfeiting protections you actually have

junior_vs_senior_signals.junior_pattern: Treats posted salary ranges as the offer itself or a ceiling; targets the midpoint to 'seem reasonable'
junior_vs_senior_signals.senior_pattern: Treats the posted range as a budget signal; explicitly targets the upper end with role-specific justification, knowing the range reflects what the employer is willing to pay
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Targeting the midpoint on a $150K–$200K range costs $25K+ annually compared to successfully anchoring at the top with supporting rationale

junior_vs_senior_signals.junior_pattern: Sits passively on a disclosed low number, hoping the employer will be generous or assuming nothing can be done now
junior_vs_senior_signals.senior_pattern: Proactively reframes in the next conversation using new information: role scope learned since, market data, or expanded responsibilities
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: A passive anchor compounds across every element of the offer; an active reframe with new information can partially or fully reset the negotiation

junior_vs_senior_signals.dimension: Framing of refusing to disclose salary
junior_vs_senior_signals.junior_pattern: Believes refusing to answer will 'hurt their chances' or signal they're hiding something; answers to avoid conflict
junior_vs_senior_signals.senior_pattern: Understands that in many states, the refusal is legally protected and professionally standard; delivers the redirect without apologizing for it
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: The social discomfort of refusing is imagined; the financial cost of answering is real and compounding across years of employment
